question: With whom does the list begin, and how many generations does the chapter cover before reaching Abraham?
Why does the text also record the sons of Ishmael, of Keturah and of Esau before going on with Israel?
In the list of the kings of Edom, the verb מוּת (mut, “die”) is repeated like a refrain: what effect does this repetition produce, and with whom does the chapter compare these kings in 1:43?
The book begins Israel's story with “Adam”: what changes when you see yourself as part of a story that begins with all humanity?
What names in this genealogy receive a comment about what they did, and what does the text say about each one?
Why does the line from Judah to David receive so much emphasis, and where does it also appear in the book of Ruth?

Achar is called the “troubler of Israel” with the verb עָכַר (akhar, “trouble”), which recalls his name and the Valley of Achor in Joshua 7: why does the Chronicler keep this memory in a list of names?
Sheshan gives his daughter to Jarha, an Egyptian servant, and the line continues through him: what unlikely people have you seen become part of God's story in your family or community?
How many sons of David are mentioned, where were they born, and which mothers are named?
Why does David's genealogy continue after Jeconiah, “the captive,” to generations after the exile?
The word בְּכוֹר (bekhor, “firstborn”) appears for Amnon and for Johanan: did either of them inherit the throne, and what does this say about the choice of kings in Israel?
The list passes through the captivity and reaches Zerubbabel: what signs of continuity do you see in the stages when everything seems interrupted?
What makes Jabez different from the names around him, and what does he ask of God?
What detail stands out in the mention of Bithiah, “Pharaoh's daughter,” within the genealogy of Judah?
The name Jabez sounds like עֹצֶב (otsev, “pain”), spoken by his mother at the birth: how does the prayer of 4:10 answer the weight of this name?
Jabez asks for protection “so that I will be free from pain”: how do you bring your fears about the future to God?
Why was Reuben, the firstborn, not counted as such, and among whom does the text divide the birthright and the leadership?
How does the chapter explain the exile of the tribes east of the Jordan, and what contrast is there with the victory of 5:20-22?
The verb בָּטַח (batach, “trust”) explains why God answered the tribes in battle: what relationship does the Chronicler draw between crying out, trusting and being helped?
They “cried out to God in the battle”: in what current struggle do you need to cry out instead of relying only on your own strength?
What families of Levites does David put in charge of the music, and who stands in the center, on the right and on the left?
What difference does the text make between the service of Aaron and his sons and that of the other Levites?
The word גּוֹרָל (goral, “lot”) appears in the distribution of the Levitical cities: why was the division made by lot, and what did this mean for the Levites, who had no territory of their own?
The singers served “according to their regulations”: what place do regularity and constancy have in your life of faith?
What kind of information is repeated in the lists of Issachar and Benjamin, and what do these counts seem to be for?
How do Ephraim's mourning and Beriah's birth interrupt the sequence of names, and what does the story of Sheerah add?
Ephraim names his son Beriah because רָעָה (raah, “disaster”) had struck his house: what does it mean to give a child a name that keeps the memory of a loss?
Ephraim's brothers come to comfort him: how have you been present in the grief of someone close to you?
What family stands out at the end of Benjamin's genealogy, and how far does the list follow its descendants?
Why does the Chronicler insist on saying who lived in Jerusalem and in Gibeon, and what link does this have with the return from exile?
Jonathan's son appears here as Merib-baal, a name containing בַּעַל (baal, “lord” or the god Baal), while in 2 Samuel he is called Mephibosheth: why might a name have been changed over time?
The tribe of Benjamin ends with “many sons and grandsons”: what inheritances, good or difficult, do you notice passing from one generation to the next?
What reason does verse 1 give for the captivity, and who are the first to return to live in the cities?
Why does the Chronicler place the list of those who returned from exile right after the genealogies and before the story of Saul and David?
The term שׁוֹעֵר (shoer, “gatekeeper”) is repeated in the description of the Levites: what tasks does the chapter assign to the gatekeepers besides guarding the entrance?
Some Levites took care of the flour, the oil, the utensils that were counted: what little-seen service do you provide, or could you provide, to your community?
How does Saul die, and what happens to his family and to the cities of Israel after the defeat?
The Chronicler sums up Saul's life in a single scene: why tell only his death, and what causes does the text point to?
The verb דָּרַשׁ (darash, “seek, inquire”) appears twice in the judgment of Saul: whom did he seek and whom did he fail to seek, and why is this verb central in Chronicles?
The men of Jabesh-gilead honor Saul even in defeat: how do you treat the memory of someone whose story ended badly?
How does David become king of all Israel, and what happens in the capture of Jebus?
Why does David pour out to the LORD the water his men brought at the risk of their lives?
The word גִּבּוֹר (gibbor, “mighty man, warrior”) marks the list: what relationship does verse 10 establish between these mighty men and the LORD's word about David?
David reigns with the “strong support” of others: who has been your support, and whom have you supported?
What special skill do the Benjamites who come to David at Ziklag have, and to what tribe were they related?
What qualities does the text attribute to the groups who come to Hebron, like those of Issachar “who understood the times,” and what do they all have in common?
The word שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) is repeated by Amasai when “the Spirit came upon” him: what does this greeting mean at that moment of distrust?
The coronation ends with food brought from afar “because there was joy in Israel”: how do you take part in the joys of your community?
How does David consult the people before bringing the ark, and how is the ark carried?
How should we understand the death of Uzzah, who seemed to want to protect the ark, in light of what 15:13 says about the first attempt?
The verb פָּרַץ (parats, “break out”) appears at the start and gives its name to Perez-uzzah: what contrast is there between the haste of the beginning and the outburst at the end?
David becomes afraid and stops, but the house of Obed-edom is blessed: what do you do when a good initiative goes wrong?
How many times do the Philistines attack, and what does David do before each battle?
Why does God give David a different strategy in the second battle, and what does it mean to wait for the “sound of marching” in the tops of the trees?
The verb שָׁאַל (shaal, “ask, inquire”) describes David before God: how does this attitude contrast with Saul's in 10:13-14?
David inquires of God again, even after winning the first time: in what situation do you trust what worked before instead of asking again?
What duties does David assign to the priests and Levites for carrying the ark?
What lesson does David draw from what happened in the first attempt, and what changes in the way the ark is carried?
The ark comes to be called “the ark of the covenant,” with the word בְּרִית (berit, “covenant”): what does this name recall about what the ark held and represented?
Michal despises David when she sees him dancing: how do you react when the joy of others in the faith seems excessive to you?
What duties does David give the Levites before the ark, and who is in charge of the first song?
The psalm of this chapter brings together passages from other psalms: what history of Israel does it recall, and why does it invite “all the earth” to sing?
The verb יָדָה (yadah, “give thanks”) runs through the chapter up to the refrain “His loving devotion endures forever”: what, according to the text, prompts this thanksgiving?
“Seek His face always”: what would it be to seek God continually in your routine?
What does David want to do, how does Nathan first respond, and what does God tell him to say that night?
What promise does God make to David about his descendants and his throne, and how was this promise read later, in Judaism and in Christianity?
The word בַּיִת (bayit, “house”) changes meaning throughout the chapter: what house does David want to build, and what house does God promise to build for him?
David asks “Who am I, and what is my house?”: how do you react when you receive much more than you expected?
Against which peoples does David fight, and what does he do with the gold, silver and bronze taken?
Why does the Chronicler mention that Solomon would make the bronze sea from the bronze of these wars?
The verb יָשַׁע (yasha, “save, give victory”) appears twice as a summary of the campaigns: to whom does the text attribute David's victories?
David “administered justice and righteousness for all his people”: what place does justice have in the responsibilities you hold?
What gesture does David make toward Hanun, and how do the Ammonite counselors interpret it?
What does Joab mean by “may the LORD do what is good in His sight,” after having planned everything for the battle?
David wants to show חֶסֶד (chesed, “loyal kindness”) to Hanun because Nahash had shown it to him: why was this gesture badly received?
The princes of Ammon distrust a good intention: when have you found it hard to believe in someone's good intention?
Where is David while Joab besieges and destroys Rabbah, and what does David receive after the conquest?
What memory of David's time do these accounts of the giants of Gath keep, and what echo do they have with the story of Goliath?
The word רָפָא (rafa, “giant,” or the name Rapha) identifies the enemies: what image do these descendants of giants convey, and how are they defeated?
The text reports without comment the harsh punishment of the Ammonites: how do you read the passages of the Bible that describe the violence of ancient wars?
Who incites David to count the people, and how does Joab react to the king's order?
In 2 Samuel 24:1 it is the LORD's anger that incites David; here it is Satan: how do different traditions read this difference between the two accounts?
The word שָׂטָן (satan, “adversary”) appears here without the article, as a proper name: what does it mean in other Old Testament texts, such as Job 1 and Zechariah 3?
David refuses to offer “burnt offerings that cost me nothing”: what offering to God costs you something?
What does David prepare for building the temple, and why does he say he needs to do this?
Why can David not build the temple, and what relationship does the text draw between Solomon's name and the kind of reign he will have?
The name Solomon is linked to שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) and to מְנוּחָה (menuchah, “rest”) in the same verse: what does this link say about the temple?
David prepares everything so that someone else can finish the work: what are you preparing that may be completed by other people?
How does David organize the Levites by number and by function?
What change does the rest given to Israel bring to the service of the Levites, who used to carry the tabernacle?
The word עֲבֹדָה (avodah, “service, work”) defines the ministry of the Levites: what concrete tasks does it include, and what does this say about the idea of worship?
The Levites were to praise the LORD “every morning” and “in the evening”: what would it be like to mark the beginning and end of your day with gratitude?
How are the priests descended from Eleazar and Ithamar divided, and who records the division?
What did the division into twenty-four courses allow in the temple service, and where do these courses reappear later, as in Luke 1:5?
The word מַחֲלֹקֶת (machaloqet, “division”) opens the chapter: what principle of organization does it express?
The lots were cast “the oldest as well as the youngest”: where could you practice this equal treatment?
What three families of musicians are set apart for the service, and how many in all were trained in the music of the LORD?
What does the text mean by calling Heman “the king's seer in the words of God,” and why does it mention the fourteen sons and three daughters God gave him?
The verb נָבָא (naba, “prophesy”) describes the work of the musicians with harps and cymbals: what relationship does the chapter suggest between music and prophecy?
The lots were cast “teacher as well as student” together: what changes when, in a group, those who teach and those who learn receive the same place?
What reason does the text give for the large number of Obed-edom's sons, and of what earlier episode does it remind us?
Why were the spoils of war dedicated by Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab and David kept for the house of the LORD?
The word אוֹצָר (otsar, “treasury, storehouse”) is repeated in the list of Levites: what care for consecrated goods does the chapter show?
Shimri was made the chief “although he was not the firstborn”: when have you seen someone chosen for their qualities, and not for their position of origin?
How is the army organized through the twelve months of the year, and where do the commanders of the divisions come from?
How do these verses take up the episode of the census in chapter 21, and why was the number not recorded in the chronicles?

The word מִסְפָּר (mispar, “number”) appears together with the promise to multiply Israel “like the stars of heaven”: what tension does the text show between counting the people and trusting the promise?
David's kingdom also depended on those who tended the vineyards, the olive groves and the herds: what ordinary work do you see as part of serving God?
Whom does David gather in Jerusalem, and what does he say about the choice of Judah, of his family and of Solomon?
What does it mean to serve God “wholeheartedly and with a willing mind,” and what warning accompanies this command?
The word תַּבְנִית (tavnit, “plan, pattern”) describes the design of the temple: to what source does David attribute this pattern, and what echo is there with the tabernacle in Exodus 25:9?
David tells Solomon “do not be afraid or discouraged”: what great work is before you now, and what gives you courage to begin it?
What does David offer from his personal treasury, and how do the leaders and the people respond to the invitation?
How does David understand the people's offering when he says “we have given You only what comes from Your hand”?
The verb נָדַב (nadav, “offer willingly”) is repeated throughout the chapter: what does it show about the people's disposition, and what does David ask God about it in 29:18?
David says we are “foreigners and strangers” and that our days are like a shadow: how can this awareness change what you do with what you own?
